meta.title: Who really said "If a man is called to be a street sweeper"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Martin Luther King Jr. — but it is not one quotation. He preached the street-sweeper image for more than a decade, from Dexter Avenue in 1954 to Barratt Junior High in 1967, and the wording changed every time. Still in copyright to 2038.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If a man is called to be a street sweeper'?
meta.ogDescription: Really King's — but no single sermon says it in the words you have read. He reworked the line for thirteen years, and the smooth version online is a composite.

answer.label: Verified — King, many times, in many wordings
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely his, and one of his favourite pieces of material. He preached the street-sweeper image for well over a decade — the earliest surviving text is a handwritten draft at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church around 1954 (a date the King Institute itself queries), another version appears in the address Facing the Challenge of a New Age at Montgomery on 3 December 1956, and the best-recorded version is What Is Your Life’s Blueprint?, delivered to schoolchildren at Barratt Junior High School in Philadelphia on 26 October 1967. What no archive contains is the exact sentence most often quoted: the tidy ‘If a man is called to be a street sweeper…’ wording is a smoothed composite of a line he kept rebuilding.

source.excerpt: If it falls to your lot to be a street sweeper, sweep streets like Michelangelo painted pictures. Sweep streets like Beethoven composed music. Sweep streets like Leontyne Price sings before the Metropolitan Opera. Sweep streets like Shakespeare wrote poetry.
trail: The strongest version is the 1967 Philadelphia one, because he was speaking to junior-high students about choosing a life, and the passage survives excerpted in Beacon Press’s edition alongside the School District of Philadelphia’s video of the address. Note the fourth name in that list — Leontyne Price, then the reigning soprano at the Met, and a Black woman from Laurel, Mississippi. She is in the sentence for a reason, and she is the first thing the internet drops the 1967 address ↗.

Eleven years earlier the same image appears in Facing the Challenge of a New Age, delivered at the First Annual Institute on Nonviolence and Social Change in Montgomery on 3 December 1956 — on the boycott’s first anniversary, three weeks after the Supreme Court affirmed Browder v. Gayle and a fortnight before the buses were desegregated on 20 December 1956. That text is published in The Papers of Martin Luther King, Jr., Volume III King Institute ↗.

The ‘like Michelangelo carved marble, like Raphael painted pictures’ wording actually belongs to The Three Dimensions of a Complete Life, delivered at the Unitarian Church of Germantown in Philadelphia on 11 December 1960 King Institute ↗. Earlier still is a handwritten Dexter Avenue draft the Institute dates only to c.1954 (with a query), and there the names are Michelangelo, Beethoven and Shakespeare — no Raphael, no marble. That is what a preacher’s recurring set piece looks like in the archive: one thought, rebuilt for each room.
source.excerptNote: The 1967 Philadelphia wording, as delivered to a room of junior-high students. It is worth reading beside the polished version in circulation: the real one is a list with a rhythm, built to be heard, and it names a living opera singer those children could have turned on the radio and heard that week.
source.rightsNote: In copyright — treat with care. King died in 1968, so his speeches and sermons run to 2038 in the United States under life-plus-seventy, and his estate is famously vigorous about enforcement: it has licensed and litigated over the speeches for decades, and won a 1999 appeal (Estate of King v. CBS) establishing that handing a text to the press was not a publication that forfeited copyright. Quoting a sentence with attribution in commentary is ordinary fair use; putting the passage on merchandise, in an advertisement or across a poster is not. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
author.heading: About Martin Luther King Jr.
author.bio: Martin Luther King Jr. (1929–1968) was a Baptist preacher first and a movement leader second, and this line is the preacher showing. Sermons are not essays: a minister builds a set piece, tests it on a congregation, keeps what lands and rebuilds the rest, and the street sweeper travelled with him from a Montgomery pulpit in 1954 to a Philadelphia school assembly in 1967. He was also, by the end of his life, working directly on labour dignity — he was in Memphis in April 1968 for the sanitation workers’ strike, supporting men who swept streets for a living.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong here
misattribution.intro: The delivery is King’s, though he credited the illustration itself to an older source. The problems are subtler: a wording that no archive contains, a missing name, an antecedent King himself named, and a widespread assumption that King’s words are free to use.

items.why: ‘If a man is called to be a street sweeper, he should sweep streets even as Michelangelo painted…’ is the version that circulates, and it is smoother than anything in the record. Delivered versions say ‘if it falls to your lot’ or ‘if your son grows up to be a street cleaner,’ and the artists change — Beethoven and Shakespeare are there from the earliest draft, Raphael and marble-carving appear in the 1960 Germantown version, and Leontyne Price arrives in 1967. Treat the polished sentence as a paraphrase.

In Philadelphia in 1967 he told the children to sweep streets like Leontyne Price sings before the Metropolitan Opera. She is almost always cut from the online version, leaving three European men. Given who he was talking to and why, that is not a neutral edit the delivered text ↗.

You will see it dated confidently to 1956, or 1967, or Strength to Love (1963). All are partly right, which is why they conflict. It is a recurring passage, not a one-off, and any citation that pins it to exactly one occasion is overstating what the archive supports.

King himself credited the street-sweeper illustration to his Morehouse mentor Benjamin Mays (King, ‘Facing the Challenge of a New Age,’ NAACP Emancipation Day Rally, 1 January 1957), and the King Institute traces the surrounding ‘be the best of whatever you are’ idea to Douglas Malloch’s 1926 poem of that name. The delivery is King’s; the trope is older.
People treat King’s words like scripture in the legal sense as well as the rhetorical one. They are not. The estate holds and enforces the copyright, and US term runs to 2038.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely King — a set piece he preached for well over a decade, best documented at Barratt Junior High School in Philadelphia on 26 October 1967, and in no single fixed wording, though King credited the illustration itself to Benjamin Mays.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It refuses the usual consolation about humble work. He does not say the job is fine, or that it is a stepping stone; he says do it at the standard of Michelangelo, which is a far harder and far more respectful thing to ask of somebody.

It also has a target. King was speaking to Black audiences in a country that had spent centuries deciding which jobs they were allowed to have, and telling them that the ceiling on the job is not a ceiling on the person.
context.detailsSummary: The same idea, thirteen years apart
detailsBody: c.1954, Dexter Avenue Baptist Church, Montgomery: a handwritten draft the King Institute dates only tentatively — sweep streets like Michelangelo painted pictures, like Beethoven composed music, like Shakespeare wrote poetry.

3 December 1956, Montgomery: ‘Facing the Challenge of a New Age,’ delivered on the boycott’s first anniversary — three weeks after the Supreme Court affirmed Browder v. Gayle and two weeks before the buses were desegregated on 20 December 1956.
11 December 1960, Unitarian Church of Germantown, Philadelphia: ‘The Three Dimensions of a Complete Life,’ where the artists become Michelangelo carving marble and Raphael painting pictures.
26 October 1967, Barratt Junior High School, Philadelphia: the fullest version, with Leontyne Price added to Michelangelo, Beethoven and Shakespeare.
April 1968, Memphis: King is in the city supporting striking sanitation workers when he is killed. The street sweeper was never a metaphor to him.
The passage remains in copyright to 2038, held by his estate.
context.pull: He does not say the job is fine. He says do it like Michelangelo.
